spoken: Think about the last task you gave a coding agent.
It made a change. You checked the work. Then you had to tell it what to do next.
Today, we will look at how to arrange those next steps in advance.
The aim is to let the work continue using evidence, with clear places to stop and review.
bridge: Before we look at an example, let me briefly explain the kind of work I do.
title: Loop Engineering

spoken: I build agent systems for everyday work, and I teach engineers how to make those systems useful.
A large part of that work starts after the first answer arrives.
We need to understand what happened, check the change, and decide what should happen next.
bridge: Let me show you a small failure that creates exactly this kind of work.
title: Harshit Tyagi

spoken: A customer asks how to handle duplicate webhook deliveries.
Then they ask a perfectly normal follow-up: ‘What should I do next?’
The search uses that short message on its own. It loses the earlier topic.
The approved webhook article exists, but the search misses it.
bridge: Who now has to figure out what went wrong and what the agent should try next?
title: Why did the assistant lose the topic?

spoken: An engineer reads the question and opens the search trace.
They ask the coding agent for a change. Then they run the checks and inspect the patch.
When another question arrives, someone has to pick up that work again.
Much of the effort is in carrying the work from one decision to the next.
bridge: Could we decide how those handoffs should work before we start?
title: What work does that failure create?

spoken: That is what we are designing when we build a loop.
We give the agent a result to reach and a way to check the current state.
We say what it may change.
Then we decide how the last result should lead to another attempt, a review, or a stop.
bridge: What would that look like with a task most engineering teams recognise?
title: What are we engineering around the agent?

spoken: Take a slow test suite.
We time the full suite, find one cause of the delay, and make a small change.
Then we run the same suite again.
If the tests pass but it is still too slow, the new timing tells us where to look next.
The result of one attempt becomes useful input for the next attempt.
bridge: What tells this loop when to begin?
title: How does a result guide the next attempt?

spoken: Sometimes we start it ourselves by submitting a goal.
Sometimes a schedule starts another check, such as an hourly check for documentation changes.
Sometimes new evidence arrives after an alert. An engineer can hand over a fixed log export and start the work.
Once a run starts, it may need several attempts. Starting a new run later is a separate choice.
bridge: Which of these ideas are we going to apply to our support assistant?
title: When should the work start again?

spoken: The support assistant has one job: find approved articles and answer the customer.
We are building an engineering loop around that assistant.
This outer loop checks saved questions, asks for a small code change when needed, and checks the system again.
A useful change waits for review. New questions can start fresh checks later.
bridge: How will we know whether one of those changes helped?
title: Which loop are we building?

spoken: We need to agree on the evidence before we start changing things.
Some checks have a clear rule. The tests pass. The expected article appears first.
Other checks need judgment. An answer can find the right article and still miss an important detail.
For our hands-on example, the automatic check will cover finding the expected source. We will review answer quality separately.
bridge: With that distinction in mind, where does another attempt create useful work?
title: What would count as better?

spoken: Look at these jobs through the work that remains.
A timing profile points to the next slow cause. A list of documentation mismatches points to the next verified edit.
A fixed error window gives us another reproducible group to investigate.
A loop helps when the last check tells us something useful about what to do next.
bridge: What do we need to write down before letting that work continue?
cue: Keep this slide brief. Slide 7 explained when work starts. This slide explains why another attempt helps.
title: Where does another attempt help?

spoken: We need five clear answers.
What starts the run? What result are we trying to reach? What may the agent change?
What will it check and save? When should it stop or wait for someone?
These choices will appear in the prompts, the feedback diagram, and the hands-on example. We are looking at the same loop in more detail.
bridge: What does this look like as a prompt we could actually run?
title: What must the loop know before it starts?

spoken: Here is the slow-test example written as an agreement with the agent.
We set a target, measure the same full suite, and ask it to work on one cause at a time.
The tests and assertions stay fixed. After every change, it repeats the measurement and saves what happened.
The highlighted fields are the values we would replace for our own project.
The last lines say when the work ends and what the reviewer should receive.
bridge: How would those instructions change if new work arrived every hour?

title: How would you ask for a faster test suite?

spoken: Now the schedule starts a fresh pass through the documentation work.
Within that pass, the agent works through verified mismatches one at a time.
It saves the last checked commit and anything still unresolved, so the next pass can continue from known state.
If there is no new work, it makes no edit. If a change already waits for review, it waits too.
bridge: What if the starting evidence comes from an alert instead of a schedule?
title: How would the docs loop find new work?

spoken: An alert gives us a fixed window of errors. An engineer starts the goal with that log export.
The agent groups duplicates, reproduces one useful case, adds a failing test, and changes one cause.
Then it reruns the checks and looks at the remaining groups.
A clear limit keeps this investigation small enough to inspect.

title: How would a loop work through errors?

spoken: Start on the left with the desired state: what we want to be true.
The controller chooses a correction. The actuator applies it to the system.
The system then produces a new result. The sensor measures that result and sends the evidence back.
We compare what happened with what we wanted. That difference guides the next decision.
This is feedback. We are choosing the next action using the result of the last one.

spoken: The first step is to make the problem visible.
An answer can go wrong before the model writes a sentence. The search may already have lost the information it needs.
We save the input, the actual search query, the returned sources, and the answer.
That gives the next attempt a specific failure to work on.

spoken: The runner connects the work between decisions.
It measures the starting state, requests a patch, runs the product tests, and checks the questions again.
It saves the results and the current state.
A bad proposal can lead to another attempt within the limits. A useful proposal waits for review.

title: 5. Workflow execution

spoken: Follow the saved history from the first measurement.
The runner selected a failure, checked the allowed changes, ran the product tests, and repeated the question checks.
It also checked the reserved questions after the patch was fixed.
Then it paused for engineering review.
Those handoffs followed the instructions we gave at the start. We did not have to write a new prompt for each one.

spoken: A reviewer can tell us whether the proposed behavior makes sense and what the checks have missed.
We read the patch and its evidence. We review the saved answer as a separate question.
If the review produces a reusable lesson, we write the approved guidance in feedback.md.
The next repair prompt reads that file.
That handoff is explicit. Saving a review reason alone does not update the repair guidance.
bridge: What would we inspect before making that decision?
title: 6. Human feedback

spoken: I would check whether the change preserves normal questions, uses the right user context, and keeps the existing checks intact.
The saved rehearsal records Codex as an automated engineering reviewer. The record keeps the reviewer and the reason visible.
In a live run, the responsible engineer records their own decision after reading the patch and the checks.
Acceptance makes the measured version the next local starting point.
Before resolving the review, let us look at what happens if another question arrives.
bridge: Should that new question interrupt a change that is still waiting for review?
cue: Show the engineering review and its reviewer type. For a fresh live rehearsal, inspect the pending patch but leave the decision open until the flow-control application on slide 30. Show the separate answer-review form without submitting a prepared verdict.
title: What should a reviewer decide?

spoken: The watcher looks for new work, but it respects the current review.
If a patch is waiting for a decision, new questions can queue up. The loop waits before making more model calls.
Once the review is resolved, it measures all active questions using the selected version of the code.
If there is a failure, it has evidence for another bounded repair. If the checks pass, it waits for changed inputs.
bridge: Can we see that happen when a new question arrives after review?
title: 7. Flow control

spoken: The first run checked six questions and proposed the shared correction.
A seventh question arrived while the review was open, so the runner waited.
After the review decision, we added a new question about choosing dates for a complete monthly usage export.
The watcher noticed the changed question set and checked all eight active questions.
The current pipeline handled them, so it made no extra code change. With unchanged inputs, the next watch pass made no model calls.
The loop took over the fresh check and the decision to wait.

title: Would you loop on a slow test suite?

spoken: A documentation loop can find a verified mismatch, update it, and rerun the build and link checks.
Those checks are useful, but they cannot fully decide whether a product claim is true.
We can let the loop work through confirmed edits while unclear claims wait for a person.
The review boundary follows what our checks can actually establish.

The smaller task gives the loop a clearer next action and a visible finish line.
